claims.text: Controlled annealing in an oxygen-controlled environment promotes formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale on Q235 steel.
A continuous, adherent oxide scale limits salt penetration and corrosion degradation at both room and high temperatures.
An optimal annealing duration produces a dense, homogeneous protective oxide film.
Insufficient or excessive oxidation produces a discontinuous or porous scale.
A discontinuous or porous scale permits rapid corrosion and mass change.
Q235 specimens will be annealed at 800 °C in 21% oxygen for 30, 60, 90, or 120 minutes.
Annealing duration will systematically alter oxide-scale formation, thickness, and continuity.
The annealed specimens will undergo cyclic corrosion exposure in Na2SO4–V2O5 at 700–900 °C, with room-temperature exposure used as a comparison.
Oxide-scale continuity, thickness, composition, and possible segregation of minor alloying elements govern protection.
An optimal oxide layer acts as a physical barrier to salt ingress.
An optimal oxide layer suppresses fast diffusion channels and thereby reduces localized corrosion.
Salt species penetrate discontinuous or porous scales more readily, accelerating degradation.
Optimally annealed specimens will exhibit lower overall mass change than non-annealed or sub-optimally annealed specimens.
Optimally annealed specimens will retain more hardness after salt exposure than the reference specimens.
Optimally annealed specimens will develop fewer localized corrosion sites than the reference specimens.
As-received specimens or specimens lacking a uniform oxide scale will show greater mass change and mechanical-property degradation during salt exposure.
The proposed relationship may not apply when impurity variation or atmosphere composition substantially alters oxidation kinetics.
The protective role of oxide scales is well established.
The optimum annealing duration may vary with intrinsic steel variability and minor compositional differences.
A lack of correlation between measured oxide-scale differences and corrosion resistance would falsify the claim that oxide-scale quality governs protection.
